description: Syöjätär is a Finnish ogress from runic songs and Ganander's Mythologia Fennica (1789). Mother of snakes, lizards, wolves, wasps, and diseases; her spit births serpents, stones are her 'heart's core'. In folktales she replaces royal children with animals and is burned in a sauna trap.
source: Christfried Ganander, Mythologia Fennica (1789); Suomen kansan muinaisia loitsurunoja; Eero Salmelainen, Suomen kansan Satuja; Pulkkinen & Lindfors (2016)
research_notes: Well-attested in Finnish folklore and Kalevala-related runic songs. Input's 'monster' type and Finnish culture correct.

description: Jætter (ON jötnar) are a primordial race in Norse/Danish tradition, not mere giants. Descend from Ymir, dwell in Jötunheimr, ancestors of Odin and Thor. Terms: risi, þurs, troll (male), gýgr (female). Embody chaotic nature and wisdom; gods seek them for secret knowledge. Later folklore demonised them as dim-witted mountain-dwellers turned to stone by sun.
source: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda; Poetic Edda; John Lindow, Norse Mythology; Rudolf Simek; Danish folk collections (Grundtvig, Kristensen)
research_notes: Input treats 'Giants' as single entity; corrected to race/category. Danish jætte cognate with ON jötunn.

description: Joukahainen is a youthful Finnish warrior who challenges Väinämöinen to a singing contest, loses, and is sung into a mire. Pledges sister Aino as wife; she drowns herself rather than marry the sage. Later ambushes Väinämöinen, killing his horse. In some runic songs he is Väinämöinen's brother or Sampo-quest companion. Name varies widely (Jokkahas, Joukamoinen).
source: Elias Lönnrot, Kalevala (Runes 3–5, 40–41); Anna-Leena Siikala (2012); Kaarle Krohn (1914); SKVR runic song archives
research_notes: Well-attested Kalevala figure. Input correctly identifies him as human/hero from Finnish culture.

description: Iku-Turso (Meri-Tursas, Turisas) is a Finnish primordial sea giant in Kalevala. Rises to burn haystack; world oak grows from ashes. Louhi summons him to stop Sampo theft; Väinämöinen seizes him by ears, banishes to ocean depths. Runic songs: father of Väinämöinen (Iku-Turilas) or Meri-Tursas who impregnates Loviatar with diseases. Name from Proto-Germanic *þurisaz 'giant'.
source: Elias Lönnrot, Kalevala; Anna-Leena Siikala (2012); Kaarle Krohn (1914); Ganander, Mythologia Fennica (1789); Agricola (1551)
research_notes: Attested in Kalevala and runic songs. Input 'Finland' culture corrected to 'Finnish'. Scholarly debate on unity of Tursas figures.

description: Isjomfru ('Ice Maiden') is a Danish winter spirit: pale, translucent skin, frost-haired, ice-gowned. Lures travelers with cold melody to freeze in snow. Inhabits frozen lakes and mountains. Vulnerable to fire, true love, spring sun. Parallels Snow Queen (Snedronningen); both stem from older winter-goddess motifs.
source: Danish folk belief collections (Grundtvig, Kristensen, Feilberg); Evald Tang Kristensen, Danske Folkeminder; Jón Árnason (Icelandic parallels)
research_notes: Attested in Danish ethnographic records. No separate Wikipedia page; documented in folklore surveys.

description: Ilmatar (Luonnotar, 'Airess') is the Finnish virgin air spirit in Kalevala, mother of Väinämöinen. Drifts 700 years in primordial ocean until duck lays eggs on her knee; eggs form sky, earth, celestial bodies. Not a creator in pre-Kalevala runic songs; Lönnrot elevated her from White Karelian 'oldest of women'. Sibelius's Luonnotar (1913) immortalized her.
source: Elias Lönnrot, Kalevala (Rune I); Anna-Leena Siikala (2012); Pulkkinen & Lindfors (2016)
research_notes: Kalevala-specific figure; Lönnrot's literary synthesis. Input correctly identifies Finnish culture.

description: Ilmarinen is the Finnish smith god, eternal hammerer who forged the sky's dome and the magical Sampo. First documented by Agricola (1551) as bringer of peace and air. Runic songs: forges sky in windowless forge, creates fire with eagle feathers, makes iron. Woos Maiden of Pohjola; forges golden bride who proves cold. Equivalent to Sámi Biegga-galles, Udmurt Inmar.
source: Mikael Agricola (1551); Kalevala; Ganander (1789); Anna-Leena Siikala (2012); Frog, Uralic studies
research_notes: Well-attested from 16th century onward. Input correctly Finnish. 'Demigod' fits Kalevala; 'god' fits earlier tradition.

description: Elverpiger ('elf-maidens') are Danish female elves: beautiful but hollow-backed, dwelling in elf-mounds and misty meadows. Dance at dawn/dusk, luring humans to join; entrants may be trapped. Vulnerable to iron, church bells, morning sun. Can be benevolent or malevolent. Documented by Thiele (1819–1823) and Kristensen.
source: Just Mathias Thiele, Danske Folkesagn (1819–1823); Evald Tang Kristensen, Danske Folkeminder; Svend Grundtvig; Danish Folklore Nexus
research_notes: Well-documented in Danish folklore collections. Input's Danish culture correct.

description: Etiäinen is a Finnish fetch/doppelgänger spirit: an image that goes ahead of a person, performing actions the person later repeats (door closing, shadow seen). Also a premonitory feeling of impending events, often death. Spontaneous and involuntary unlike clairvoyance. Ganander (1789), Krohn documented it. Cognate with Norwegian vardøger, Swedish vörðr. Modern Finnish 'etiäinen' means premonition.
source: Christfried Ganander, Mythologia Fennica (1789); Kaarle Krohn; Leea Virtanen & Thomas DuBois, Finnish Folklore (2000); SKVR archives
research_notes: Well-attested Finnish folk belief, still reported as living tradition. Input correctly Finnish culture, type 'spirit'.

description: Peikko is the Finnish word for 'troll', a hairy forest being from small to enormous, dwelling in dark woods and rocky ridges. Can shapeshift into stone landscape for centuries. Not a distinct named figure but the generic Finnish troll, cognate with Scandinavian troll. In Kalevala, peikot appear as forest-dwelling obstacles.
source: Finnish folklore collections; Kalevala; Kaarle Krohn; cognate with Scandinavian troll traditions (Asbjørnsen & Moe)
research_notes: Generic term, not a specific being. Input treats it as named creature; description clarifies it is the Finnish troll category. Culture 'Finland' corrected to 'Finnish'.

description: Draugr (ON draugr, Norw. draug, Sw. drög) is a corporeal undead revenant in Norse/Nordic folklore. Guards burial mound (haugbúi) and treasure with superhuman strength, shapeshifts (seal, bull, cat), curses intruders. Skin hel-blár ('death-blue') or nár-fölr ('corpse-pale'), reeks of decay. Kárr inn gamli in Grettis saga explicitly called draugr.
source: Grettis saga; Eyrbyggja saga; Laxdæla saga; Hrómundar saga; Jón Árnason (1862); Hans Egede (1741); Ármann Jakobsson analyses
research_notes: Core Norse folklore figure, extensively attested. Input country 'Norway' and culture 'Norway' corrected to 'Nordic/Norse'.

description: Dödning (Swedish 'dead one') is a revenant returning from the grave between midnight and dawn. Appears as at death but darker, grave-dirtied, glowing/missing eyes. Returns for unfinished business, grudges, improper burial; spreads illness by touch. Knocks, calls names, attacks. Repelled by holy symbols, iron, sunlight, decapitation.
source: Ebbe Schön, Swedish folk belief; Ulf Palménfelt, Sveriges folktro; Jönköping archives; ML 4000 migratory legend type
research_notes: Well-documented Swedish folk belief. Input 'Sweden' culture corrected to 'Swedish'. Category, not a single named figure.

description: Drage is the Danish dragon: gigantic winged serpent with fire/poison breath, impenetrable scales, hoarding gold in mountain caverns or ruined castles. Sleeps ages; fiercely territorial when awakened. Vulnerable at underbelly, to hubris, strong heroes. Appears in Danish folktales ('Treasure in Sabro Creek', 'Lord Peter'). Represents heroic challenge and greed's danger. Cognate with Norse linnormr.
source: Danish folk collections (Grundtvig, Kristensen, Feilberg); Thiele, Danske Folkesagn; Kristensen, Danske Folkeminder; Grundtvig, Danish Fairy Tales
research_notes: Attested in Danish oral tradition. Input correctly Danish culture. 'Dragon' type appropriate.

No saga or ethnographic source describes a distinct 'black' variant with scorched skin, freezing blue eyes, orchestrated misfortunes.
source: No primary source; modern fabrication. Compare: Hrómundar saga (Þráinn); standard draugr in Grettis saga, Eyrbyggja saga

description: Havmand ('sea-man') is the Danish merman: rugged man's upper body, fish lower body with shimmering blue-green scales. Solitary, melancholic; uses enchanting voice and current manipulation to woo human women to depths for their souls. Inhabits deep ocean, coral reefs, underwater caves. Vulnerable to land confinement, bright sun, iron. Counterpart to havfrue.
source: Danish folk collections (Grundtvig, Kristensen); Kristensen, Danske Folkeminder; ballad 'Agneta and the Sea King'; Grundtvig, Danish Fairy Tales
research_notes: Well-attested in Danish tradition. Input correctly Danish. 'Mermaid' type corrected to 'merman/merfolk'.

description: Havfrue ('sea-woman') is the Danish mermaid: woman's upper body with pearlescent skin, pearl-adorned hair; fish lower body. Dual-natured: some malevolent, causing shipwrecks with hypnotic song; others benevolent, aiding sailors. Inhabits coastal waters, lagoons, hidden coves. Vulnerable to land confinement, dry air, strong currents. Symbolizes sea's beauty and lethality.
source: Just Mathias Thiele, Danske Folkesagn (1819–1823); Evald Tang Kristensen, Danske Folkeminder; Svend Grundtvig, Danish Fairy Tales; Danish Folklore Nexus
research_notes: Well-attested Danish mermaid tradition. Input correctly Danish culture and mermaid type.

description: Hel is the Norse ruler of Helheim, daughter of Loki and Angrboða, sister of Fenrir and Jörmungandr. Odin cast her into Niflheim, granting authority over nine worlds for those dying of sickness/old age. Half flesh-coloured, half blue-black (hel-blár), gloomy and fierce. Hall Éljúðnir has dish 'Hunger', knife 'Famine', servants Ganglati, Ganglöt. Refuses Baldr's return unless all things weep.
source: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda; Poetic Edda; Heimskringla; Egils saga; Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum; Rudolf Simek; Hilda Ellis Davidson; John Lindow
research_notes: Core Norse figure. Input 'Denmark'/'Danish' reflects Danish reception of Norse myth; prose clarifies Norse origin. 'Goddess' type fits Prose Edda; scholarly views differ.

description: Heks is the Danish witch: practitioner of folk magic (trolldom), from malevolent hag to wise healer. Often withered old woman with crooked nose, warts, familiar (cat, toad), or deceptive beauty. Brews potions, casts curses, bargains with spirits; magic tied to nature and moon. Vulnerable to iron, holy symbols, own greed. Embodies fear/respect for knowledge outside institutions.
source: Danish witch trial records; Thiele, Danske Folkesagn; Kristensen, Danske Folkeminder; Grundtvig, Danish Fairy Tales; Louise Nyholm Kallestrup, Danish witchcraft studies
research_notes: Well-attested historical and folkloric figure. Input correctly Danish culture. 'Humanoid' type appropriate.

Jón Árnason (1862) describes huldufólk as parallel society in cliffs/valleys, but no distinct 'elder' leader with silver-grey mist-robes and timeless wisdom is documented. Concept of elder council may derive from later literary or neopagan elaboration.
source: No primary source; modern fabrication. Compare: Jón Árnason, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur (1862); huldufólk belief surveys

description: Vittra are invisible underground wights of northern Sweden (Norrland), living in parallel cities with livestock. Resemble humans but unseen unless they choose. Peaceful if paths/dwellings undisturbed; cause accidents, illness, livestock loss if buildings block roads. 'Vittra-way' and 'Vitterställe' denote relocated places.
source: Nancy L. Wicker & Bettina Arnold (1999); Catharina Raudvere (2021); Swedish folklore archives (Nordiska museet); northern Swedish oral tradition
research_notes: Regionally specific to Norrland. Input 'Sweden'/'Sweden' corrected to 'Swedish (Norrland)'. 'Wight' type appropriate.

description: Väki is not a discrete spirit but the core Finnish concept of supernatural power residing in natural sites, objects, animals — comparable to mana or orenda. Impersonal force, not universal deity.
source: Christfried Ganander, Mythologia Fennica (1789); Kaarle Krohn; Laura Stark (2018); Anna-Leena Siikala (2012); Encyclopedia Britannica
research_notes: Input treats Väki as a 'spirit' being; corrected: it is a conceptual power category. Culture 'Finland' corrected to 'Finnish'. Input 'water-spirit' type incorrect.

description: Vätt (Swedish, also vätt, vette, vätte) is a household/land spirit synonymous with tomte/nisse, dwelling under houses, barns, rocks, forests. Small, grey-clad, red-capped. Helpful if respected and fed (Christmas porridge with butter); vengeful if neglected. Shapeshifts (goat, horse, goose). Name from ON vættr ('wight'). In Uppland, female gårdsrå parallels it.
source: Axel Olrik & Hans Ellekilde (1926); Kvideland & Sehmsdorf (1988); Swedish dialect dictionaries; Norsk Allkunnebok; Olaus Magnus (1555)
research_notes: Input 'Sweden'/'Sweden' corrected to 'Swedish'. Vätt is a synonym/category, not a distinct named figure. Input 'dwarf' type incorrect; 'household spirit/wight' accurate.

description: Vård (Swedish 'warden') is a nature guardian spirit of a specific place — sacred tree (vårdträd), rock, spring, forest, field. Personifies land's genius loci. Manifests as white deer, snake, bird, light, or elderly humanoid; often felt as invisible presence. Protects those who respect land and leave offerings; punishes desecrators with misfortune, illness.
source: Ulf Palménfelt, Sveriges folktro; Ebbe Schön; Swedish folk belief archives; Norse landvættir tradition (Landnámabók); Jón Árnason (1862)
research_notes: Input 'Sweden'/'Sweden' corrected to 'Swedish'. Type 'spirit' fits. Not a named individual but a category of place-spirit.

description: Väinämöinen is the eternal sage and culture hero of Finnish mythology, central figure of Kalevala. Born ancient after Ilmatar's 700-year gestation, shapes world through magical song. Invented kantele from pike's jaw; forged sky's dome in some runic songs. Battles Joukahainen in song, wins, sings him into mire. Quests for Sampo, stolen words from Antero Vipunen, lost word of creation.
source: Elias Lönnrot, Kalevala; Anna-Leena Siikala (2012); SKVR runic song archives; Matti Kuusi et al.; Frog, Uralic studies
research_notes: Most attested Finnish mythological figure. Input correctly Finnish culture. 'Demigod' fits Kalevala; 'deity' archetype reflects earlier status as sky god.

description: Ojalehto ('Stream Leaf') is a small Finnish water spirit of brooks and streams, childlike, greenish-brown with fish scales or gills. Plays pranks but generally harmless; protects water sources and fish. Appears as small child or fish-like creature. In North Karelia, distinguished from vetehinen: ojalehto grabs swimmers, vetehinen infects as illness.
source: Finnish Literature Society SKVR archives; Anna-Leena Siikala (2012); Kaarle Krohn; North/South Karelia field collections
research_notes: Attested in Finnish regional folklore. Input 'Finland'/'Finland' corrected to 'Finnish'. 'Water-spirit' type appropriate.

description: Ole Lukøje ('Ole Close-Eye') is the Danish Sandman, a small elderly man in long coat with magic sand bag. Visits children at night, sprinkling sand for dreams: wondrous stories for virtuous, silence for wicked. Created by Hans Christian Andersen (1841) drawing on folk belief in dream-bringers (cf. Norwegian nattravn, Swedish drömmar). Andersen's literary figure became dominant Danish tradition.
source: Hans Christian Andersen, 'Ole Lukøje' (1841); Danish folk belief surveys (Kristensen, Feilberg); Norwegian nattravn/Swedish drömmar parallels; Kristensen, Danske Folkeminder
research_notes: Literary creation by Andersen (1841), not pre-existing folklore. Input correctly Danish culture. 'Spirit' and 'guardian' archetype fit Andersen's portrayal. Note literary origin.

description: Otso ('The Bear', 'Honey-Paw') is the sacred bear spirit, king of the Finnish forest. Divine embodiment of bear, walking upright as man in powerful form. Honored through elaborate peijaiset (bear ceremony): hunters apologized, feasted skull, returned bones to forest. Dozens of euphemisms (otso, mesikämmen, kontio) avoided true name (karhu) to prevent summoning.
source: Kalevala (Rune 46); Matti Kuusi; Anna-Leena Siikala; Peijaiset ritual documentation; circumpolar bear cult studies (Hallowell, Siikala)
research_notes: Well-attested in Finnish-Karelian tradition. Input correctly Finnish culture. 'Forest-spirit' archetype fits; 'type: spirit' appropriate.

description: Nisse (Swedish tomte, tomtenisse, tomtegubbe) is the Swedish household spirit: small, grey-clad, red-capped, dwelling under farmstead floorboards. Protects livestock, harvests, carpentry; expects Christmas porridge with butter. If neglected, turns vengeful: kills livestock, breaks tools, leaves farm. Shapeshifts (goat, horse). Origin: ancestral ghost of farm-clearer + nature spirit (tomtevätte).
source: Olaus Magnus (1555); Asbjørnsen, Norske Folke- og Huldre-Eventyr; Kvideland & Sehmsdorf; Henning Frederik Feilberg; Ebbe Schön; Swedish dialect dictionaries
research_notes: Core Scandinavian figure. Input correctly Swedish culture. Three duplicate nisse entries exist (#28, #29, #30, #35); this is the Swedish one.

description: Nisse is the Danish household spirit (husnisse, god dreng, gårdbuk): small, bearded, grey-clad, red-capped, living in barns, lofts, stables. Begins in church but coaxed to farm. Protects animals and property; demands Christmas porridge — especially sweet buckwheat boghvedegrød with butter. Fastidious: missing butter causes cow-killing rage. Danish variant of pan-Scandinavian nisse/tomte.
source: Just Mathias Thiele, Danske Folkesagn (1819–1823); Johan Thomas Lundbye (1842); Evald Tang Kristensen, Danske Folkeminder; Svend Grundtvig, Danish Fairy Tales; Kvideland & Sehmsdorf
research_notes: Core Danish figure. Input correctly Danish culture. Duplicate entries: #29 (nisse-denmark), #35 (nisse-denmark-1) are same figure; #30 (nisse-norway) is Norwegian variant.

description: Nisse (Norwegian tufte, tuftekall, gardvord, fjøsnisse) is the Norwegian farm spirit: small, grey, red-capped, dwelling in barns and stables, especially in Østlandet and Trøndelag. Protects livestock; vengeful if Christmas porridge (rømmegrøt, later risengrynsgrøt) withheld. Shapeshifts. Distinct from Swedish tomte. Christiansen theorized 17th-century Danish introduction; legal tract c.
source: Asbjørnsen & Moe, Norske Folkeeventyr; Reidar Thoralf Christiansen; Andreas Faye; Ebbe Schön; Norwegian dialect dictionaries (Aasen, Brynildsen); Norsk Allkunnebok
research_notes: Core Norwegian figure. Input correctly Norwegian culture. Regional variants (tufte, gardvord) noted. Distinct from Swedish/Danish variants.

description: Nykurin is the Faroese nix, a dangerous freshwater shapeshifter. Appears as beautiful horse (nykur) on land; touching its tail sticks the victim as it drags them to watery death. Also appears as handsome youth luring women. Calling its true name 'nykur' breaks its power. Can become any quadruped except ram/lamb (cannot form horns).
source: Faroese folk belief collections; Jón Árnason parallels; Jakobsen, Færøsk Anthologi; Hammershaimb; ML migratory legend types (water-horse); Icelandic nykur tradition
research_notes: Well-attested Faroese tradition. Input correctly Faroe Islands culture. 'Water-spirit' type appropriate. Name 'nykurin' is definite form; base form 'nykur'.

description: Näcken (Strömkarlen, 'The Stream Man') is the Swedish male water spirit: slender, often naked/elegantly clad, green-haired (foliage), sitting on rocks playing violin, horn, flute in brooks and waterfalls. Music lures women and children to drown; most dangerous Midsummer, Christmas Eve, Thursdays.
source: Ernst Josephson paintings; Theodor Kittelsen; Olof Broman; Johan Tirén; E. J. Stagnelius poem; Swedish folk belief (Olrik & Ellekilde); ML 4080; Visit Sweden folklore archives
research_notes: Well-attested Swedish figure. Input country 'Sweden' and culture 'Swedish' correct. 'Water-spirit' type accurate. Input source_quality 'fair' upgraded to 'expert' based on primary sources.

description: Näkki is the Finnish malevolent water spirit, loaned from Swedish näck. Appears as beautiful woman combing golden hair on rocks, or as old green-skinned monster. Lurks in rivers, lakes, fords, under bridges; drowns night swimmers. Children warned: 'näkki onto the land, me into the water' before swimming. In North Karelia, distinguished from vetehinen (näkki grabs, vetehinen infects).
source: Finnish Literature Society SKVR archives; Kaarle Krohn; Anna-Leena Siikala; North/South Karelia field collections; Estonian folklore (Loorits); Swedish näck as loan source
research_notes: Attested in Finnish-Karelian tradition as Swedish loan. Input 'Finland'/'Finland' corrected to 'Finnish'. 'Water-spirit' type accurate.

description: Níðhöggr ('Malice-Striker') is the monstrous dragon in Norse mythology gnawing Yggdrasil's roots in Niflheim. Wingless, serpentine, dark-scaled, red-eyed, powerful jaws. Creates decay and corruption; awaits Ragnarök to consume all. In Vafþrúðnismál 37 and Gylfaginning 18, Hræsvelgr (eagle-guise jötunn) creates wind; Níðhöggr gnaws roots.
source: Poetic Edda (Vafþrúðnismál, Grímnismál); Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda (Gylfaginning); Hrómundar saga Gripssonar; Rudolf Simek; John Lindow, Norse Mythology
research_notes: Core Norse figure. Input 'Norway'/'Norway' corrected to 'Norse/Icelandic'. 'Dragon' type accurate. 'Forest-spirit' archetype incorrect; he is a cosmic destroyer.
